title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined with a logical-OR scoring rule, and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline implemented under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and the same candidate was replayed to both arms (baseline is therefore not an independent-generation condition). The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300 (shared candidate). Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); validators never reported forbidden reachability and the repair step was never invoked. Paired risk-difference = 0.0, McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Observing 0/300 violations gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was not exercised, this study quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract; it does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We archive the preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to guide follow-up stress tests designed to exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) offer pragmatic routes to automate intent-driven network configuration, but operator communities rightly worry that generated artifacts may expand attack surface, violate access-control policies, or otherwise introduce security-relevant regressions. System and survey research thus emphasizes constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as operational mitigations [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W4415071524]. However, rigorous, preregistered confirmatory evidence that a verifier placed in the loop meaningfully reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations under adversarial inputs is scarce.

We designed, preregistered, and executed a paired experiment to answer a focused operational question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Our study makes four evidence-grounded contributions: (1) a machine-readable preregistration that fixes a paired N = 300 confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1); (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution that used two deterministic validators combined with a logical-OR decision rule and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract to conserve model calls; (3) full execution and analysis artifacts showing a degenerate confirmatory result (n11 = 300) together with a post-hoc descriptive Clopper–Pearson upper bound on undetected baseline violation rate (≈0.00994); and (4) artifact-grounded operational recommendations and reproducibility materials to inform future stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path. All experimental artifacts (preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis outputs) are archived in the evidence bundle to enable independent verification.
sections.related_work:
Prior work motivates our design along three lines. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have demonstrably improved correctness for code and Infrastructure-as-Code tasks by using execution or verifier feedback to direct repair; such systems (e.g., TerraFormer and related verifier-feedback approaches) demonstrate that verifier power and repair strategies are decisive for realized gains [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. Second, surveys and NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch—and consistently recommend integrating validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce operational risk [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Third, emulation and testbed work shows execution-based validation is feasible for research-grade evaluation but warns of external-validity gaps when porting to production devices or live traffic [https://openalex.org/W4406170828].

What is less explored in the verified literature is a preregistered paired evaluation that (a) fixes generation semantics, (b) quantifies the trade-off between model-call budget and inferential power, and (c) archives deterministic per-episode verifier traces to support auditability. Our study fills that precise niche by combining a paired confirmatory design, deterministic validators, and explicit shared_initial_candidate semantics to trade compute for reproducible accounting.
sections.methodology:
Preregistered confirmatory design: The study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1 specified a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds + 150 programmatic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in the proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). The confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). Prespecified CIs were to be computed by a bootstrap percentile method; final analysis used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729 (this change is logged in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Sampling, deduplication, and contamination handling followed the preregistration: exact duplicates and fuzzy duplicates (normalized edit distance < 0.15) were removed prior to execution, and any high-overlap items were flagged for sensitivity checks (see analysis/contamination_summary.csv).

Adapter contract and generation semantics: To limit model-call cost under the execution contract, we preregistered and executed a shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired intent one initial LLM candidate is generated and the same candidate is replayed to both arms (baseline and guarded). This choice yields exactly one hosted-model generation per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) instead of two independent draws per pair, thereby reducing provider usage (maximum_model_calls = 600 allowed by the contract). The execution manifest's provider-call audit records stage_counts: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300. Importantly, because baseline is a replay of the shared initial candidate rather than an independent sample, baseline is not an independent-generation condition; this reduces the probability of observing discordant violating outputs across the pair and therefore limits the ability of the paired McNemar test to evaluate repair efficacy (see Results). We make this contract explicit here and cite execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json for verification of model_calls_used and the shared_initial_generation accounting.

Intervention arms and repair policy: Baseline = the shared initial candidate replayed directly; Guarded = same initial candidate validated by deterministic validators and, if any validator reports forbidden reachability, allowed up to one repair LLM call according to the preregistered repair policy (max one repair per pair). The repair invocation rule and the repair prompt template are archived in the transformation manifest and per-episode validator_trace records. Repair attempts are only triggered by a validator-detected forbidden-reachability predicate; across the run no repair prompt was issued because validators never flagged forbidden reachability.

Validators, scoring rule, and determinism: Two deterministic validators were used (one containerized Batfish-style execution validator and a lightweight static reachability analyzer). For scoring we combined the two validators with a logical-OR decision rule: a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports the forbidden-reachability predicate. This combination rule and the per-episode validator outputs are recorded in execution/scoring/*.json (validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version = '5.0') and are cited here to enable verification of both the decision rule and the per-episode repair_applied flags. The environment (Dockerized FRRouting-style images, deterministic orchestration) and sampling seeds are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl to ensure deterministic replay of the experiment under the same adapter contract.

Analysis plan and prespecified sensitivity: Primary inference used a McNemar paired test on complete matched pairs; secondary reporting included 95% bootstrap percentile CIs (final analysis used 10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The preregistration specified sensitivity analyses treating technical/model failures as violations; no technical failures occurred (analysis/missingness_summary.csv records zero failures). All per-episode raw responses, validator traces, and the provider-call audit are archived as the reproducibility backbone (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/responses/, execution/execution_manifest.json).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit: The run completed planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions) with completed = 600 and failed episodes = 0. Provider-call accounting under the shared_initial_candidate contract shows model_calls_used = 300 (maximum_model_calls in the contract = 600). The execution manifest records the run interval (started 2026-08-28T22:15:28Z; completed 2026-08-28T22:50:41Z) and the provider-call stage 'shared_initial_generation' = 300. Representative per-task artifacts (execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json) demonstrate the shared-candidate playback pattern and deterministic validator traces.

Primary confirmatory outcome: All 300 complete pairs passed the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). The paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0. The prespecified bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg).

Interpretation of degenerate contingency: With n11 = 300 and n10 = n01 = 0 the McNemar test is uninformative about repair efficacy because no discordant pairs exist for the paired binary test to compare. This is a direct, quantitative consequence of two coupled design facts recorded in the artifacts: (a) the shared_initial_candidate contract reduced independent-sample variance between arms, and (b) none of the programmatic adversarial variants triggered a validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the chosen model and validators. Observing 0 violations in N = 300 independent episodes yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability of 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%); we report this numeric bound as a descriptive constraint on undetected baseline violations (computed from the archived per-episode outcomes, analysis/condition_summary.csv).

Repair activity and verifier concordance: Because validators never reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate, no repair call was invoked and all per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied flags are false. Per-episode traces show validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true in every archived scoring artifact; verifier_disagreement_rate across the two validators is 0 in the analysis artifacts (analysis/contamination_summary.csv and per-episode scoring files show concordance). The absence of repair activity implies the experiment tested whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant under the chosen contract, not whether verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations.

Representative examples: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json illustrate a typical medium-difficulty transition (shutdown_configure_restore pattern) where the shared candidate matches the reference answer and validator_trace reports no violations. Additional representative tasks and scoring traces are archived to permit spot-checking of parsing, normalization, and validator judgments.
sections.discussion:
What this evidence supports: Under the exact adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), model (declared: gpt-5-mini), validator set (two deterministic validators combined by logical OR), emulator, and programmatic adversarial perturbation generator used here, baseline generation already satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for all sampled intents; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The archival artifacts unambiguously support that statement: provider-call accounting (execution/execution_manifest.json), per-episode validator_trace entries (execution/scoring/*.json), and the paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) are mutually consistent.

What this evidence does not show: Because the repair path was never invoked, the experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction; the degenerate observed contingency violates that assumption and renders the confirmatory McNemar inference moot for repair efficacy. Researchers should therefore not interpret the null paired difference as proof that verifiers are unnecessary in all deployments.

Design lessons and operational recommendations grounded in artifacts: (1) Generation semantics matter: the shared_initial_candidate contract reduces model calls (model_calls_used = 300 vs up to 600 for independent draws) but also reduces independent-sample variability needed to produce discordant violations that repair might correct. For experiments meant to exercise repair efficacy, we recommend independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or increasing repair-call budgets; the execution manifest archives the cost trade-off (maximum_model_calls = 600) and thus supports budgeting decisions. (2) Adversary potency matters: programmatic adversarial perturbation used here (one deterministic variant per benign seed, archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl) did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for this model/validator configuration; stronger adversaries or targeted perturbations against verifier predicates should be used to exercise repair paths. (3) Verifier strength and diversity matter: we evaluated two deterministic validators combined by logical OR; future studies should include multiple oracle families and production-grade oracles to stress different failure modes. (4) Reproducibility is practical: per-episode raw responses, validator traces, provider-call audit, and the analysis log (including bootstrap parameters and seed) are archived in the evidence bundle and permit exact replication of the reported accounting and contingency outcomes.

Threats to validity (artifact-grounded): Internal validity is limited by the shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope (execution/model_configuration.json and deterministic_reconciliation.json show single-model runs and shared generation). Construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators adequately model operational security risk; we record validator IDs and versions for independent assessment (execution/scoring/*.json). External validity is limited because tasks were synthetic and executed in deterministic Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation and may not cover production device heterogeneity (execution/task_manifest.jsonl documents the emulator composition). Conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency is degenerate and the preregistered power assumptions are not met. All these threats and their artifact locations are enumerated to support transparent reanalysis and targeted follow-up tests.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation with a declared LLM (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not exercised and the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs. The results emphasize that generation semantics (shared vs independent draws), adversary design, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity materially determine whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to inform follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl, and the transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
